identity.title: Chest pain radiating to both arms (or right arm/shoulder), with diaphoresis

technique.how: Ask where the pain travels and have the patient point: to the left arm only, the right arm/shoulder, or both arms. Separately ask about, and look for, sweating at the time of pain (observed diaphoresis carries more weight than reported).
technique.prerequisites: Reliable history; record radiation site before the ECG result biases the interviewer.

interpretation.positive_finding: Radiation to both arms is specific for ACS (pooled specificity 96%, LR 2.6) and for MI (LR 7.1 in the 1998 RCE); observed sweating has pooled LR+ 2.9 for AMI.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of bilateral-arm radiation or sweating is common in ACS and barely lowers the probability.
interpretation.pitfalls: Left-arm-only radiation adds little. The high 7.1 estimate comes from older MI cohorts and is not reproduced in the 2015 pooled ACS analysis; do not treat as diagnostic.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: raise pretest probability for ACS and proceed promptly to ECG/troponin pathway. Negative: no change; ACS remains in play.

estimates.population: ED patients with chest pain suggestive of ACS (prospective studies 1995-2015)
estimates.reference_standard: Final hospital diagnosis of ACS or cardiovascular event within 6 weeks
estimates.quote: pain radiation to both arms (specificity, 96%; LR, 2.6 [95% CI, 1.8-3.7])

estimates.population: Patients with acute chest pain (studies summarised in the 1998 RCE)
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of MI per included studies (ECG/enzymes)
estimates.quote: chest pain radiating to both the left and right arm simultaneously (LR, 7.1)

estimates.population: 893 ED chest pain unit patients with acute undifferentiated chest pain; 3.8% AMI
estimates.quote: pain radiating to the shoulder or both arms (LR = 4.07)

estimates.population: Non-selected patients with chest pain (16 of 28 studies; primary care and ED)
estimates.quote: Sweating had the highest pooled positive likelihood ratio (LR+), namely 2.92 (95% CI = 1.97 to 4.23) for acute myocardial infarction

sources.citation: Fanaroff AC, Rymer JA, Goldstein SA, Simel DL, Newby LK. Does This Patient With Chest Pain Have Acute Coronary Syndrome? The Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review. JAMA. 2015;314(18):1955-1965.
Panju AA, Hemmelgarn BR, Guyatt GH, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient having a myocardial infarction? JAMA. 1998;280(14):1256-1263.
Goodacre S, Locker T, Morris F, Campbell S. How useful are clinical features in the diagnosis of acute, undifferentiated chest pain? Acad Emerg Med. 2002;9(3):203-208.

Bruyninckx R, Aertgeerts B, Bruyninckx P, Buntinx F. Signs and symptoms in diagnosing acute myocardial infarction and acute coronary syndrome: a diagnostic meta-analysis. Br J Gen Pract. 2008;58(547):105-111.
Swap CJ, Nagurney JT. Value and limitations of chest pain history in the evaluation of patients with suspected acute coronary syndromes. JAMA. 2005;294(20):2623-2629.
Body R, Carley S, Wibberley C, McDowell G, Ferguson J, Mackway-Jones K. The value of symptoms and signs in the emergent diagnosis of acute coronary syndromes. Resuscitation. 2010;81(3):281-286.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of radiation or sweating to lower suspicion; do not apply to patients with aortic dissection features (tearing pain, pulse deficit) where arm symptoms have a different meaning.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Bilateral-arm radiation with diaphoresis is a high-probability ACS pattern: immediate ECG, troponin, aspirin unless contraindicated, and monitored bed.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Reliability of radiation history not reported in retrieved sources; observed versus reported sweating differ (Body 2010 used observed sweating).

extraction_notes: Fanaroff 2015 pooled ACS estimate and Bruyninckx 2008 pooled sweating estimate come from abstracts (no PMC full text). Panju 1998 LR 7.1 is given without CI in the abstract; number of underlying studies not visible. Right-arm/shoulder-specific LR (Swap 2005 Table, ~4.7) could not be viewed and is not entered; Goodacre's 'shoulder or both arms' LR 4.07 is entered instead. Body 2010 reports adjusted odds ratios (both arms 2.69; sweating observed 5.18), not LRs, so it is cited but no estimate entered.
